The Pendulum and the Restoring Force

For the last few lectures, we talked quite a bit about how we can do data analysis more like a pro. Today, we are going to get back into more of the paper-and-pencil knowledge that helps us understand the physical world.

Let’s picture a pendulum swinging back and forth. One thing that is pretty easy for us to picture is its displacement as a function of time, which we will call x(t). This is the horizontal distance from the center—or, if you want to be fancy, the equilibrium position. Obviously, this displacement oscillates and changes with time t.

A week or so ago, we went through the physics behind this, drawing a free-body diagram and figuring out which way the relevant forces point. We ended up with what we call a second-order ordinary differential equation (ODE), which looks like this: \begin{equation} \frac{d^2}{dt^2}[x(t)] = -\omega^2 x(t) \tag{1} \end{equation}

We get this from the physical point of view because, just like we learned in the rally car unit, when you take the second derivative of displacement with respect to time, you get acceleration. That acceleration (or the net force acting on the pendulum’s mass) comes from just one type of force: the restoring force. It is called a restoring force because every time we displace the mass farther away from the center, the more it wants to come back toward the center. The restoring force increases with displacement.

Aside: Are you blocking your head because you just realized you could have taken a nap? You can still do that, but I’ll be watching. I think it takes some guts, right?

For now, we are ignoring friction or damping—this is just the restoring force, pure and simple.

Let’s also talk about this character, \omega. It is not a “w”, and as my 10-year-old might say, it looks a bit like a butt, but it is the Greek letter omega. This represents the angular frequency. You might be familiar with standard frequency—how many times something goes back and forth in a second, measured in Hertz. We call \omega the angular frequency because it has units of radians per second. The larger the value of \omega, the more quickly the mass is oscillating. We can relate it to the period T (the time it takes for one full swing from left to right and back) with this simple equation: \begin{equation} \omega = \frac{2\pi}{T} \tag{2} \end{equation}

From our physical derivation of the pendulum, we learned that this angular frequency depends on both the gravitational acceleration g and the length of the pendulum L: \begin{equation} \omega = \sqrt{\frac{g}{L}} \tag{3} \end{equation} We verified this in gory detail with our data analysis, showing that this expression holds to a very good approximation.

The Universal Harmonic Oscillator

This mathematical framework doesn’t just apply to pendulums. Any function whose second derivative is equal to the negative of its angular frequency squared multiplied by that same function is called a harmonic oscillator.

Can you think of some other examples of things that oscillate?

  • Mass on a spring: If you have a block of mass m sitting on a smooth, frictionless surface attached to a spring with stiffness k, its horizontal displacement follows the exact same differential equation. The only difference is that gravity and length are irrelevant here. Instead, the angular frequency depends on the stiffness and the mass: \omega = \sqrt{k/m}. A stiffer spring means faster oscillations; a heavier mass means slower oscillations.

  • Atomic Force Microscopy (AFM): In a nano class, you might have seen an AFM cantilever that vibrates up and down, kind of like a diving board by a swimming pool. The displacement of that AFM tip is governed by the same ODE.

  • Magnetic Resonance (NMR/MRI): If you apply a magnetic field B to a nuclear spin, the magnetic moment will precess (rotate) around the axis, like a spinning toy top. The transverse magnetic moment along the x-axis, M_x, follows this same second-order ODE. The angular frequency of this precession is \omega = \gamma B, where \gamma is the gyromagnetic ratio (a constant that depends on the material).

  • LC Circuits: Is there anybody here who likes electrical circuits? ... I see someone vigorously shaking their head. Okay, no circuits! But just for the sake of completeness, in an LC circuit with an inductor (inductance L) and a capacitor (capacitance C), the electrical charge Q stored on the capacitor oscillates back and forth. The charge behavior is described by the same ODE, with an angular frequency of \omega = 1/\sqrt{LC}.

You could even imagine this applying to population dynamics, where a population overshoots and undershoots an equilibrium level due to some biological restoring force. The point is: while we derived this equation for a swinging pendulum because it was easy to experiment with in the classroom, the harmonic oscillator is a universal concept that applies to countless physical systems.

A quick warning about that square root: if you swap in a block that is twice as heavy on your spring, the angular frequency does not get cut in half. The mass sits under a square root in the denominator, so doubling m divides \omega by \sqrt{2}. The system definitely oscillates more slowly, but it is not a simple linear drop.

Solving Differential Equations: Guess and Check

My job for the next couple of days is to help you understand this harmonic oscillator. It is one step up from the first-order differential equations we learned, but we can apply a lot of the same ideas.

One major idea is that, from this point on in the class, we will never try to solve a differential equation directly. We did it once with our first-order ODE, which looked like this: \begin{equation} \frac{d}{dt}[f(t)] = r f(t) \tag{4} \end{equation} where f(t) is some arbitrary function and r is a growth rate constant. We performed direct integration to figure out that the solution was exponential growth: f(t) = C e^{rt}, where C is an integration constant.

Going forward, we are going to use a route called substitution and differentiation. All we are going to do is hypothesize (or guess) what the function is, plug it back into the differential equation, and see if it is legit.

Does that sound like sacrilege to anybody? That we aren’t going to “solve” the equation, just guess the solution? To me, it doesn’t! Let me give you an analogy. Let’s say we have a simple algebra equation: \begin{equation} 6x + 7 = 67 \tag{5} \end{equation} (The numbers here are entirely coincidental). We have all done algebra since middle school, so we know how to solve this directly: \begin{align*} 6x &= 67 - 7 \\ 6x &= 60 \\ x &= 10 \end{align*}

But what if a 10-year-old were to look at this? They wouldn’t know algebra yet, but a smart 10-year-old knows how to multiply and add. They could figure out that they need to find a number x that, when multiplied by 6 and added to 7, gives 67. They can just guess and check!

  • Try x = 1 \rightarrow 6(1) + 7 = 13 \neq 67 (Nope)

  • Try x = 100 \rightarrow 6(100) + 7 = 607 \neq 67 (Nope)

  • Try x = 10 \rightarrow 6(10) + 7 = 67 = 67 (Yep!)

You can still be smart without knowing algebra. Because solving differential equations directly gets really hard beyond the first order, we are going to act like that smart 10-year-old. We will guess a function and check if it works.

Let’s verify our guess for the first-order ODE. We hypothesize that f(t) = C e^{rt}. Let’s plug it into the left side of Equation 4 and differentiate: \begin{align} \frac{d}{dt} \left[ C e^{rt} \right] &= C \frac{d}{dt} \left[ e^{rt} \right] \nonumber \\ &= C \left( r e^{rt} \right) \nonumber \\ &= r \left( C e^{rt} \right) \nonumber \\ &= r f(t) \tag{6} \end{align} It matches the right side of the ODE! So f(t) = C e^{rt} is a legit function that works.

Guessing the Solution for the Harmonic Oscillator

Now, as grown folks, let’s look at our second-order ODE (Equation 1). We need a mystery function x(t) that, when differentiated twice, gives us the exact same function back, just multiplied by -\omega^2.

What are our choices? What functions do you know that return to their original form after two derivatives, but pick up a negative sign?

If you shouted out “sine” or “cosine,” you are spot on. Let’s test a sine function. We will guess: \begin{equation} x(t) = A \sin(\omega t) \tag{7} \end{equation} where A is the maximum amplitude. Let’s take the first derivative. In calculus, you learned that the derivative of sine is cosine. The only trick is that the \omega stuck inside the parentheses has to pop out front (chain rule): \begin{equation} \frac{d}{dt}[x(t)] = A \omega \cos(\omega t) \tag{8} \end{equation}

Now, let’s differentiate this first derivative again to get the second derivative. The derivative of cosine is negative sine, and once again, another \omega pops out front: \begin{align} \frac{d^2}{dt^2}[x(t)] &= \frac{d}{dt}[A \omega \cos(\omega t)] \nonumber \\ &= -A \omega (\omega) \sin(\omega t) \nonumber \\ &= -A \omega^2 \sin(\omega t) \tag{9} \end{align}

Let’s rearrange this slightly by swapping A and \omega^2: \begin{equation} \frac{d^2}{dt^2}[x(t)] = -\omega^2 \left( A \sin(\omega t) \right) \tag{10} \end{equation} Notice that the term in the parentheses is exactly our original guess, x(t)! So we can rewrite this as: \begin{equation} \frac{d^2}{dt^2}[x(t)] = -\omega^2 x(t) \tag{11} \end{equation} Voila! It works out beautifully. Sine is a legit solution.

Cosine would work just as well. In fact, there is no guarantee that your oscillation starts exactly at zero or exactly at the maximum amplitude. To capture that, you can tack on a little fudge factor inside the parentheses, called a phase factor, \phi: \begin{equation} x(t) = A \cos(\omega t + \phi) \tag{12} \end{equation}

For our pendulum, which one should we choose? If you pull the pendulum away from its center to a maximum displacement and let it go at t=0, it makes the most natural sense to use cosine, because cosine starts at its maximum value. So, we will proceed with x(t) = A \cos(\omega t). (And if instead you let the pendulum hang at rest and gave it a swift kick at t=0, the displacement starts at zero, so sine would be the natural pick. The phase factor \phi lets you slide smoothly between those two extremes.)

Graphical Intuition for Derivatives

You can always just memorize the fact that the derivative of sine is cosine, and the derivative of cosine is negative sine. But I want to show you a quick graphical way to internalize why that is, and why that \omega has to pop out front. If you have multiple color pens, this is the time to pull them out!

Let’s draw our displacement function, x(t) = A \cos(\omega t). It starts at a maximum displacement A, swings down through zero to -A, and comes back up. It takes one period, T = 2\pi/\omega, to complete one cycle.

Finding Velocity Graphically

Now, let’s find the first derivative graphically. The first derivative of displacement is velocity, v(t). Remember that taking a derivative just means calculating the slope of the curve at that point.

Here is the trick:

  1. First, check out where the slope of the displacement is exactly horizontal. That happens at the peaks and valleys (maximum and minimum displacement). At these points, the slope is zero, so the velocity must be zero.

  2. Next, look at where the curve has the steepest slope. That happens exactly halfway between the peaks and valleys, right as the displacement crosses zero.

  3. As the pendulum swings from positive A down to negative A, it crosses zero with the steepest negative slope. So, our velocity graph should hit its most negative value there.

  4. As it swings back from negative A to positive A, it crosses zero with the steepest positive slope. So, our velocity graph should hit its most positive value there.

In the figure below, the top panel is the red displacement curve with those tangent lines drawn in (green = flat, orange = steepest), and the bottom panel is the velocity curve we build from them. The gray dashed lines are your “drop-down” guides: pick a time on top, slide straight down, and read off the velocity.

If we connect these dots, we get a smooth, sinusoid-like curve. It starts at zero, goes negative, comes back to zero, goes positive, and returns to zero. This is the exact mirror image of a standard sine wave, which means it is a negative sine wave!

But why do we have this \omega out front? Why is the amplitude A\omega instead of just A? The steepness of the slope depends on how big \omega is. If you have a small \omega (a long period), the mass oscillates really slowly, so the slope is very gentle (small velocity). If you have a big \omega (a short period), the mass whips back and forth quickly, creating a much steeper slope (large velocity). The multiplier \omega out front is the mathematical way of capturing that physical reality.

Seeing the \omega: Same Amplitude, Different Steepness

Here is the picture that makes that argument concrete. Both panels below show a cosine with the same amplitude A—the mass travels the same distance either way. The only thing I changed is \omega. On the left, \omega is small, so the period T = 2\pi/\omega is long and the curve takes its sweet time getting from +A down to -A. On the right, \omega is doubled, the period is cut in half, and the curve has to cover the same vertical distance in half the time. The orange tangent line at the zero crossing is the slope you would measure, i.e., the peak speed.

Read it like this: the mass has to cover the vertical drop 2A in a quarter-period-ish stretch of time. Shrink the time axis (big \omega), and the same drop happens over a narrower horizontal window, so the tangent tips toward vertical. In symbols, the peak speed is \begin{equation} |v|_{\max} = A\omega = \frac{2\pi A}{T} \tag{13} \end{equation} Double \omega and you double the steepness; halve \omega and the tangent flattens out. That is the entire reason an \omega pops out front every time you differentiate \sin(\omega t) or \cos(\omega t)—the chain rule is just bookkeeping for “how fast is the clock inside the parentheses ticking?”

Taking it One Step Further: The Second Derivative

Instructor Note: We ran out of time in class to cover this final step, so I am filling in the gap here!

We just found the first derivative (velocity). Now, let’s apply the exact same graphical logic to the velocity curve to find the second derivative, which is acceleration, a(t).

Look at the blue velocity curve above.

  1. At t=0, the velocity is zero, but its slope is heading downwards—it is at its steepest negative slope! Therefore, the acceleration at t=0 must be at its most negative value.

  2. At t=T/4 (the first valley of the velocity curve), the velocity is at its most negative, but the curve is flat. The slope is zero. So, acceleration is zero.

  3. At t=T/2 (crossing zero velocity), the slope is at its steepest positive angle. So, acceleration is at its maximum positive value.

Here is the same side-by-side treatment as before, except now the blue velocity curve is the “parent” on top, and the orange acceleration curve is the “child” we build underneath. Same color code: green tangents are flat, orange tangents are steepest.

If we plot these points and connect them, we get a curve that starts at a negative maximum, goes to zero, rises to a positive maximum, and comes back down.

Look at the shape of this orange acceleration curve. It is a cosine wave, but flipped upside down. It is exactly the negative of our original red displacement curve! And because we took the derivative of a curve that already had an amplitude of A\omega, another \omega pops out, making the amplitude of the acceleration A\omega^2.

Accuracy Note

Possible error: This contradicts the amplitude relationship established in the same paragraph, where the acceleration’s amplitude is stated to be A\omega^2 while the displacement’s amplitude is A. The two curves are not "exactly" negatives of each other unless \omega = 1; they share the same shape/phase but differ in amplitude by a factor of \omega^2.

Correction: The acceleration curve has the same shape (a flipped cosine) as the displacement curve, but its amplitude is A\omega^2 rather than A, so it is only proportional to the negative of the displacement (via a(t) = -\omega^2 x(t)), not identically equal to its negative.

Mathematically, we just showed graphically that: \begin{equation} a(t) = -A\omega^2 \cos(\omega t) \tag{14} \end{equation} Since x(t) = A\cos(\omega t), we can substitute x(t) right back in: \begin{equation} a(t) = -\omega^2 x(t) \tag{15} \end{equation} And there it is! The graphical method brings us full circle right back to our original second-order differential equation. The acceleration is always opposite to the displacement, pulling the system back toward equilibrium.
